newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metals plants seek return to profit in 1997.
newsitem.headline: German metals plants seek return to profit in 1997.

text.p: German metals industry association WVM on Thursday said producers would aim to reduce unit and labour costs in 1997 in order to return to profitability after a weak 1996.
They would increase capacity utilisation by lengthening shifts, shed staff and stress the development of new materials.
WVM chairman Jochen Schirner said this was the answer to unsatisfactory profit margins at the 600 WVM companies, which produce and process metals in the world's third largest metals industry.
Sales in 1997 should improve from 37.7 billion marks in 1996, which were seven percent off from the previous year.
Early 1997 orders from the electrical and machine-building industries, car manufacturers and packaging, were looking up.
But producers were expecting staff costs to rise by one percent in 1997 and two percent in the wake of unfavourable wage negotiations.
The industry was worried by ecologically-inspired calls to block the use of metals in certain building and packaging applications, Schirner said.
It was also unhappy about the restrictions placed on scrap trade flows from so-called Basle convention rules, which define certain scraps as waste rather than industrial raw materials.
Schirner said German taxes and fees, environmental and energy costs needed to be cut, otherwise the industry would continue its exodus to countries less hostile to its activity.
He named the Netherlands, Luxembourg, France, Spain and overseas countries.
WVM had pledged to cut energy consumption by 22 percent in the 1990-2005 period to reduce carbon dioxide emissions.
